name: Eat like a bodybuilder (rice/chicken/broccoli)

lead: Chicken, rice and broccoli is the traditional bodybuilding plate, eaten in planned portions to build muscle or lose fat. The payoff is a more muscular, leaner physique with very few daily food decisions.

The chain is high protein plus measured carbohydrate, which makes calorie intake easy to control: a surplus with enough protein supports muscle gain alongside training, and a deficit supports fat loss. The three-food menu itself hasn't been trialled, but calorie balance and protein intake are widely covered in sports nutrition.

paras: People cook large batches and repeat the same meals across bulking phases (eating above maintenance) and cutting phases (eating below it), adjusting portions of rice and protein. Competitive bodybuilders start cutting roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest, and visible changes build over weeks to months alongside lifting.

Risks depend on the amounts and on extreme contest-prep methods such as dehydration. Very repetitive menus can limit variety and be hard to sustain, and individual needs differ, so people with medical conditions or a history of disordered eating may want professional guidance.

angle.text: The rice, chicken and broccoli template is used to gain muscle or cut fat with very few food decisions, building a leaner, more muscular physique. High protein and measured carbs make calorie control easy, and calorie control plus training is what changes body composition. The principles are well studied in sports nutrition; the three-food menu is a convention.

lead: Eating like a bodybuilder usually means building meals around a lean protein such as chicken breast, a measured portion of rice or another slow-digesting carbohydrate, and a green vegetable such as broccoli. People adopt it to gain muscle or lose fat in a controlled way: predictable foods make calories and protein easy to count, and muscle mass and leanness drive the broad shoulders, defined arms and visible abs that appearance-focused lifters want.

Wikipedia describes competitive bodybuilders alternating between a bulking phase, in which they eat a calorie surplus to build muscle, and a cutting phase, in which they eat a deficit to lose fat while keeping as much muscle as possible. Cutting typically starts about 12 to 14 weeks before a contest. Chicken, turkey, beef, fish, eggs, dairy and slow-digesting carbohydrates are the staple foods named. The pattern has roots in the physical culture and contest scene of the early twentieth century and in the diet-focused magazine culture of the 1950s and 1960s.

The rice, chicken and broccoli pattern has become shorthand for this style of eating on fitness forums and social media, alongside meal prep. On looksmax.org it is both a default recommendation and a frequent target of debate about whether it supplies enough variety, fat and micronutrients.[1][2] No clinical trial has tested this exact meal set; the principles behind it, calorie balance and protein intake, are studied in sports nutrition, where a 2018 meta-analysis of 49 trials found protein supplementation increased fat-free mass and strength during resistance training.[3]

paras: Bulking means eating in a calorie surplus, and the larger the surplus or the longer the bulk, the more fat is added alongside muscle. Cutting means eating in a deficit to lose fat; larger deficits work faster but raise the risk of losing muscle. Wikipedia distinguishes dirty bulking, a large surplus often built from junk food without tracking macronutrients, from clean bulking, which aims to add muscle with little fat, takes longer and relies on tracking calories and macronutrients.

The rice, chicken and broccoli template fits clean bulking and cutting because each food is easy to weigh and log. A typical plate has a lean animal protein, a measured portion of a starchy carbohydrate and a green vegetable. Variations swap in turkey, white fish, eggs, potatoes, oats or other vegetables, and some lifters add lean beef or oily fish for fat and micronutrients. In the fitness world the pattern is often combined with meal prep, the practice of cooking a week of portioned meals in advance, which Wikipedia says can standardise portion sizes and appeals to people who want to lose weight or gain muscle.[4]

Chicken is the most produced meat in the world according to Wikipedia, and raw boneless breast provides about 22 g of protein and about 2 g of fat per 100 g, compared with about 20 g of protein and 9 g of fat in raw flank steak.[5] That ratio is why breast meat became the default bodybuilding protein. The same page notes that raw chicken can carry Salmonella and that US health authorities advise cooking it to an internal temperature of 165 F (74 C).[5]

White rice, per Wikipedia's figures, supplies about 130 kcal, 28.6 g of carbohydrate and 2.4 g of protein per 100 g cooked, and rice is not a complete protein; brown rice keeps the bran and germ that milling removes.[6] Lifters value it as a compact, cheap carbohydrate that is easy to digest around training.

Broccoli provides about 34 kcal and 2.6 g of fibre per 100 g raw, with very high vitamin C and vitamin K contents, and it contains glucosinolates that break down into compounds such as sulforaphane; Wikipedia says boiling substantially lowers glucosinolate levels while steaming, microwaving or stir-frying do not.[7] In the bodybuilding template it adds volume, fibre and micronutrients for few calories, which helps with fullness during a cut.

The diet is a product of bodybuilding's history rather than of one inventor. Modern bodybuilding grew from the physical culture movement: Eugen Sandow staged his Great Competition at the Royal Albert Hall in 1901, and Bernarr Macfadden promoted a large American contest at Madison Square Garden in 1903 to 1904. The Weider brothers founded the IFBB in 1946 and the Mr. Olympia contest began in 1965. Wikipedia says diet became a central focus in the 1950s and 1960s, when magazines spread advice on bulking up and cutting down along with protein and other food supplements.

Supplement history ran alongside. Wikipedia's supplement article says Sandow promoted dietary control in the 1910s, that Irvin P. Johnson popularised egg-based protein powders in the 1950s, and that the supplement industry grew rapidly in the 1970s and 1980s.[8] Whole-food staples such as chicken, fish, eggs and rice sat beside those products.

Not every influential coach favoured a high-carbohydrate plate. Vince Gironda (1917 to 1997), the Los Angeles trainer nicknamed the Iron Guru, promoted a low-carbohydrate, high-fat steak and eggs diet built on red meat, eggs, butter and cream, and his trainees included Larry Scott, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Frank Zane and Lou Ferrigno.[9] Steve Reeves (1926 to 2000), regarded as one of the most influential bodybuilders, is credited with popularising bodybuilding worldwide.[10] Rice-based, low-fat eating and Gironda-style low-carbohydrate eating are two long-running schools within the same culture.

The Wikipedia bodybuilding article cites recommendations of 25 to 30 percent of calories from protein and notes disagreement over intake, with positions ranging from about 1 gram per pound of body weight per day to 1.5 to 2 grams or more. Protein is commonly spread across the day and placed around workouts. For comparison, the US and Canadian recommended dietary allowance is 0.8 g per kg of body weight for a typical sedentary adult, and Wikipedia gives about 1.4 to 1.8 g per kg for strength athletes and up to 1.8 to 2.0 g per kg for athletes restricting calories.[11]

A 2018 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine pooled 49 randomised trials with 1,863 participants and found that protein supplementation during at least six weeks of resistance training increased strength and fat-free mass, with no further fat-free mass gain at total intakes above about 1.6 g per kg per day; the benefit was larger in people with prior training experience.[3] A 2020 review by Roberts, Helms, Trexler and Fitschen suggests 1.8 to 2.7 g per kg of protein for physique athletes in contest preparation, 10 to 25 percent of calories from fat with carbohydrate filling the remainder, four or five protein doses a day, and weight loss of no more than 0.5 percent of body mass per week.[3]

Bodybuilders usually favour low-glycaemic, slow-digesting carbohydrates, and some take fast sugars such as dextrose or maltodextrin around training to refill muscle glycogen. Many eat five to seven meals every two to three hours, which helps manage large food volumes on a bulk and limits overeating on a cut. Wikipedia adds that studies comparing meal frequency show no metabolic-rate advantage over three meals a day. A 2026 ISSN position stand on diets for weight reduction concluded that meal frequency does not crucially affect fat loss,[3] and a 2026 cross-sectional study of 320 adults found no significant difference in fat or muscle percentage between small frequent meals and three regular meals.[3] A 2023 survey of 33 bodybuilding coaches found they commonly advised 3 to 7 meals a day and at least 2 g per kg of protein.[3]

Competitors typically bulk for most of the year and then cut for about 12 to 14 weeks before a show; final-stage strategies include carbohydrate loading and dehydration for definition and vascularity. A case study of one natural male bodybuilder followed a 26-week preparation with a calorie-restricted diet, more cardio and continued lifting: body weight fell from about 88.6 kg to 73.3 kg and body fat from 17.5 to 7.4 percent, with improved resting heart rate, blood pressure and arterial stiffness; the authors note that one case cannot establish general effectiveness.[3]

A 2026 narrative review of body recomposition found that resistance training combined with protein of about 1.6 to 2.4 g per kg per day is the most consistent strategy for gaining muscle while losing fat, with larger effects in untrained and higher-fat individuals and smaller effects in trained or lean people.[3] A 2025 scoping review of 73 expert documents from 14 organisations found common guidance on energy surplus or deficit and protein across four to six feedings, while noting that fats, fibre and micronutrients received little attention and wording was often vague.[3] That last point is the research counterpart of the forum debate about narrow menus.

On looksmax.org the bodybuilding meal is discussed as a staple of gym-focused users, and it draws criticism from others. One thread, whose title uses the word slave, argues that rice, broccoli and chicken as the only foods can leave diets short on animal fat and micronutrients, claims rice carries heavy metals and broccoli contains plant defence chemicals, and suggests adding fattier meats and other animal foods; replies in the same thread say chicken itself is a good protein source but not ideal as the sole meat.[1] A separate thread complains that chicken is not nutritionally dense and takes large portions to feel full, with a reply favouring beef for micronutrients.[2] A light-hearted thread celebrates broccoli, with the poster describing buying it in bulk each week.[12]

Supporters of the pattern point to its simplicity and low cost; critics on the forum focus on variety and fat intake. These are opinions from forum participants rather than study results. The Wikipedia bodybuilding article cites academic work on fitness influencers, #fitspiration and muscularity-oriented social media, which sits behind how bodybuilding-style eating spreads online.

No trial has tested rice, chicken and broccoli as a combined diet for appearance outcomes. Related research looks at the protein source. A meta-analysis of 36 randomised trials with 1,803 participants compared diets containing red meat with diets in which it was replaced by plant proteins, poultry, fish, mixed animal protein, refined carbohydrate or the usual diet, measuring blood lipids and blood pressure, and reported no significant differences between red meat and all comparison diets combined.[13] A randomised controlled trial in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition compared red meat, white meat and non-meat protein sources on atherogenic lipoprotein measures under low and high saturated-fat intake.[14]

Wikipedia notes that dirty bulking can increase body fat and, over time, affect cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity, that large calorie deficits risk muscle loss, and that contest-style dehydration is a late-stage practice for competitors. Wikipedia also says high protein intake has no established tolerable upper limit and no conclusive evidence of causing chronic kidney disease, while people with kidney disease are generally advised to reduce protein.[11] The forum criticism noted above concerns variety and nutrient coverage on a narrow menu.[1]

Rigid eating is a recognised concern in the sport. Muscle dysmorphia, a form of body dysmorphic disorder also called bigorexia, involves strict nutritional regimens, supplementation and overtraining; Wikipedia reports a 1993 study of 108 male bodybuilders by Pope, Katz and Hudson as an early description, with prevalence estimates of 1 to 54 percent of men in studied samples.[15] A 2026 survey of 60 competitive bodybuilders reported frequent weight monitoring and post-competition binge eating in both sexes, a 2026 narrative review proposed that weight-tracking apps and social media may reinforce dietary rigidity, and a 2025 meta-analysis of 10 studies linked muscle dysmorphia symptoms to obsessive-compulsive traits and to anabolic steroid use.[3]
No studies found on rice, chicken and broccoli as a dietary pattern. Related trials and meta-analyses of protein intake, meat protein sources and blood lipids are described above.[13][14][3]

lore.intro: The meal is discussed on looksmax.org as the standard gym diet, with debate about whether it is nutritionally complete.[1][2]
